original_question: What is the reverse-mathematical strength of the following statement: for every finite graph G and every k >= 2, every coloring of all copies of G in the Rado graph into countably many colors, with each color used at most k times, has a subgraph isomorphic to the Rado graph in which no two copies of G receive the same color?
target_in_paper: The open reverse-mathematics problem asking for the strength, over RCA_0, of the statement that the Rado graph is rainbow Ramsey; in the surrounding official source this is the reverse-mathematical question attached to the theorem that the random/Rado graph U(2,2) is rainbow Ramsey.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly captures the core combinatorial principle: a countable copy of the Rado graph, a fixed finite graph G, a coloring of all copies of G into countably many colors, a k-boundedness hypothesis on the coloring, and the conclusion that there is a subcopy of the Rado graph on which the coloring becomes injective on copies of G.
missing_details: The reverse-mathematical setting should be stated explicitly: the paper asks for the strength over the base theory RCA_0.
The paper’s formal shorthand is that the Rado graph is rainbow Ramsey; the long statement should be tied to that definition.
“Copies of G” should be specified as induced copies / finite induced substructures in the graph-theoretic presentation used by the source.
The coloring is a function into ω, and “k-bounded” means every color class has size at most k.
To be presentation-independent in reverse mathematics, one should say “for every countable graph R isomorphic to the Rado graph” or otherwise fix a coded presentation of the Rado graph.
The quantifier order should be explicit: for every finite G, for every k, for every k-bounded coloring γ, there exists a subcopy R' ≅ R such that γ is injective on copies of G inside R'.
The nearby official open question also asks for a comparison with Ramsey’s theorem and with the rainbow Ramsey theorem for pairs of natural numbers.
If one wants the closest paper-faithful wording to the explicitly numbered reverse-mathematics question in the surrounding source, the special case of edges is the one singled out there.
refined_question: Over RCA_0, what is the reverse-mathematical strength of the assertion that the Rado graph is rainbow Ramsey: namely, that for every countable graph R isomorphic to the Rado graph, every finite graph G, every natural number k >= 1, and every k-bounded coloring γ from the set of induced copies of G in R into ω, there exists an induced subgraph R' of R with R' ≅ R such that γ is injective on the induced copies of G in R'?  How does this principle compare in strength with Ramsey’s theorem and with the rainbow Ramsey theorem for pairs of natural numbers?
justification: The arXiv note 1808.10227 is a short problem list about reverse mathematics, so the formal combinatorial content behind this item must be read from the underlying rainbow-Ramsey source it points toward. In that source, Definition 1.1 gives the exact meaning of “rainbow Ramsey” for a countable structure via k-bounded colorings into ω and injectivity on a subcopy; Section 3 identifies U(2,2) with the random/Rado graph; Theorem 5.2 proves that U(2,2) is rainbow Ramsey as part of a more general theorem; and the reverse-mathematical problem is then asked explicitly in the concluding questions, including comparison with Ramsey’s theorem and the rainbow Ramsey theorem for pairs. Your draft is therefore substantively right, but it omits the base theory RCA_0, the induced-substructure formulation, and the comparison clause that is part of the official question.
